assertions.interpretation_note: Preserves U.S. acceptance-record wording distinguishing the people of Uruguay from government actors.
Smithsonian identifies the Washington recast's founder as unknown in Montevideo, Uruguay; no agent is inferred.

Smithsonian describes the Washington sculpture as a recast of the 1898 Artigas sculpture; Uruguay's heritage resolution independently identifies Washington among foreign bronzes copying the San José monument.
Smithsonian identifies the Washington recast's founder location as Montevideo, Uruguay; the recast date is represented separately as its own assertion.
Approximate date is retained as a separate checkable claim rather than embedded in prose.
Uruguay's heritage resolution states that the San José commission entrusted realization of the statue to Juan Luis Blanes in 1894.
After Juan Luis Blanes died, Juan Manuel Blanes developed the sketch that served as the basis for Dante Costa's work.
Uruguay's heritage resolution records Dante Costa's contractual modeling/plaster/casting role and states that he cast the bronze in his Florence workshop.
The 1924 congressional report says the people of Argentina presented the statue; later U.S. sources vary between citizens, people, and Government of Argentina.
The 1924 congressional authorization expressly calls the Washington work a copy of the San Martín statue; the National Register record likewise describes it as a copy of the Buenos Aires work.
The National Register documentation records disassembly for Metro construction and relocation/rededication at the Virginia Avenue site in 1976.
Buenos Aires city government and Argentina's Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano identify Louis-Joseph Daumas as sculptor of the 1862 Buenos Aires equestrian statue.

Argentine official sources identify Louis-Joseph Daumas as author of the Washington copy and describe Washington among copies of the Daumas statue. Multiple U.S. federal records instead identify Augustin-Alexandre Dumont. Publish the conflict rather than silently selecting the U.S. catalog attribution.

NCPC describes the urn as a gift from the Government of Cuba, while the National Register nomination describes it as a gift from citizens of Cuba. Machado's presidential direction and presentation are separately established. Preserve the donor-label conflict.
National Register documentation says the urn was a gift from citizens of Cuba to the people of the United States; NCPC instead labels the sponsor Government of Cuba.
The urn was carved from a physical fragment of a marble column of the Havana Maine Monument. This is material provenance, not merely design lineage.

National Register documentation separately states that the urn's relief/compositional elements derive from Felix Cabarrocas' Havana Maine Monument. This design relationship is distinct from reuse of its marble.
National Register documentation identifies engineer Felix Cabarrocas as winner of the design competition for the Havana Maine Monument.

The National Register nomination explicitly lists the urn's architect/builder as unknown and states that the urn's sculptor is unknown. Do not infer Felix Cabarrocas as urn sculptor from his authorship of the predecessor monument.
